newsitem.title: INDONESIA: One killed in attack at East Timor cathedral.
newsitem.headline: One killed in attack at East Timor cathedral.

text.p: At least one person was killed in an attack at the cathedral in East Timor's capital of Dili on Tuesday as thousands waited for afternoon mass to be said by Nobel peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, residents said.

Two people were seriously injured in another incident at Dili's Komoro airport, where tens of thousands of East Timorese had gathered since dawn to greet Belo on his arrival back home from a trip to Europe, they said.
"We saw at least one person dead at the cathedral," a resident said.
A staff member at the Wirahusada military hospital in Dili confirmed that one person had died and five had been admitted with injuries, some serious. He refused to give details.
Staff at Dili's general hospital said no one had been admitted there after the incidents.
Residents said the man at the cathedral, wearing plain clothes, was attacked by youths after he was found carrying a pistol and a walkie-talkie radio.
Witnesses said the crowd stretched around six km (four miles) from the airport. "There was more than 100,000 people," a resident said.
The official police estimate was 5,000. Local journalists put the figure at between 30,000 and 150,000.
One resident said the two men in civilian clothes who were attacked at the airport had their car burnt after the crowd saw a rifle, pistol and grenades in the vehicle.
"There were many people attacking them and a priest who tried to stop (them) had his white cassock covered in blood," he said.
He said rumours had been rife in Dili in recent days of an imminent attack on Belo. Last month Belo said there had been two attempts on his life in 1989 and 1991.
Colonel Atok Rismanto, deputy East Timor police chief, told Reuters three armed forces members had been taken to hospital with wounds after the crowds attacked them in a "brutal" action.
Rismanto said the incidents were under investigation and that nobody had been detained.
"Generally, the atmosphere had been very joyful that the bishop had returned from his trip safely," one resident said.
Belo had travelled to Norway to receive his Nobel prize and had also met Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Germany and Pope John Paul II at the Vatican.
American congressman Patrick Kennedy, on a two-day visit to East Timor, arrived on the same midday flight with Belo.
Belo later said a mass where he called for unity.
"Let us be united even if we have differences of opinions or concepts," Belo told the congregation.

Residents said that despite the disturbances, preparations for Christmas celebrations in the mostly Catholic former Portuguese colony were continuing. A number of foreign diplomats were expected to attend the events.

Predominantly Moslem Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975. It declared the enclave its 27th province the following year in an act never recognised by the United Nations, which regards Portugal as the administering power.
In November 1991, troops shot dead at least 50 protesters who were on their way to a cemetery in Dili following the funeral of an anti-Indonesian activist killed two weeks earlier.
World attention refocused on East Timor in October when Belo jointly won the Nobel prize with self-exiled East Timorese independence activist Jose Ramos Horta.
